extracted.intended_audience: administrators in the South African public service (administrators required to comply with the Promotion of Administrative Justice Act)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for public-service administrators on identifying ‘administrative action’ under the Promotion of Administrative Justice Act (AJA), following procedural-fairness obligations, giving reasons, drafting decisions/letters, handling internal remedies and judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'administrative action' (six elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative action means a decision (or failure to take a decision) that: (a) is of an administrative nature made in terms of an empowering provision; (b) is not specifically excluded by the AJA; (c) is by an organ of state; (d) adversely affects rights; and (e) has 'direct external legal effect'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Guide summarises section 1 of the AJA into these elements and then examines each element in detail. Use this checklist to decide whether the AJA applies to a particular act.

rubrics_metrics.name: A 'decision' includes failures to decide
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative action includes a decision or a failure to take a decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to make a decision (e.g., failing to decide on a passport application) can adversely affect rights and therefore count as administrative action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of acts that qualify as 'decisions'
rubrics_metrics.description: A decision can be making, suspending, revoking or refusing to make an order/award/determination; giving/suspending/revoking/refusing certificates, directions, approvals, consents or permissions; issuing/suspending/revoking/refusing licences or other instruments; imposing conditions or restrictions; making declarations, demands or requirements; retaining or refusing to deliver up an article; or doing/refusing to do any other act of an administrative nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When determining whether an act is a decision, check whether it fits one of these listed categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Must be made in terms of an 'empowering provision'
rubrics_metrics.description: For a decision to be administrative action it must be of an administrative nature and made by an administrator pursuant to an empowering provision (a law that grants the power to make the decision).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always identify the statutory/regulatory provision that authorises the decision (e.g., Minister’s power in the Passports Act). If no empowering provision exists, the AJA does not apply to the act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusions: actions 'specifically excluded' by the AJA
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain actions are excluded from the definition of administrative action and so are not governed by the AJA, including policy decisions of the executive, the making of legislation by Parliament/provincial legislatures/municipal councils, and the exercise of judicial functions by courts and some bodies; decisions under the Promotion of Access to Information Act are also excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the action falls into an exclusion category (e.g., purely policy choice, legislative acts, judicial functions, PAIA decisions), follow the separate legal regime rather than the AJA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action by an 'organ of state' (and entities exercising public power)
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative action must be by an organ of state (departments, police, parastatals, municipal councils, functionaries or institutions exercising powers under legislation). The AJA can also apply to private individuals/companies when they exercise public power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether the actor is an organ of state or is exercising public power on behalf of the state (e.g., outsourced contractors). The Guide notes that private-sphere application can be ignored for many practical purposes, but legally such acts may be captured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adversely affects rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision must adversely affect rights — impose a burden, limit or remove rights, or be an adverse determination that a person does not have a right (beneficial decisions generally are not adverse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider direct deprivations (withdraw licence) and determinations (refuse licence). Also recognise that granting a benefit to one person can adversely affect another (e.g., competing applicants). Rights may arise from the Bill of Rights, legislation, contract or promises by administrators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Has 'direct external legal effect' (legal, direct and external components)
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative action must (i) have legal effect (a legally binding determination of rights/obligations), (ii) be direct (final step that affects the public), and (iii) be external (affects persons outside the internal daily operations of the organ of state, though individuals within the organ affected in their individual rights are included).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If only intermediate internal steps are taken, only the final step may have direct effect. Example distinctions: supervisor instruction (internal, not administrative action) vs suspension of a public servant (external, administrative action).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural fairness requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 33(1) and the AJA require administrative action to be lawful, reasonable and procedurally fair. Procedural fairness includes giving affected persons an opportunity to be heard (audi), adequate notice, and fair impartial decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Guide distinguishes two kinds of administrative action requiring procedural fairness: decisions affecting any person (section 3) and decisions affecting the public (section 4). Procedural fairness obligations include telling people about proposed action, allowing representations, and specifying the nature/purpose of proposed action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audi alteram partem — communicating with the applicant (notice & opportunity to respond)
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrators must inform affected persons of findings and planned decisions and give them a fair opportunity to explain/represent before a final decision is taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communication can be by writing, telephone or other channels, but written procedures are usually best. The Guide provides a model letter that sets out what to tell the applicant and a clear deadline for reply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum requirements for a written decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Every written decision must contain: a clear decision (including particulars), adequate reasons (or information on the right to request reasons), and information on any legal remedies available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are minimums — more complex decisions require more detailed reasons. The Guide provides a template and describes where to be succinct or elaborate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of a decision (template parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: A suggested decision structure: (i) address block (addresses, date, reference), (ii) state the problem/purpose, (iii) the main decision in one sentence (no reasons), (iv) subordinate decisions (one sentence each), (v) cost order if applicable, and (vi) reasons for the decision including jurisdiction, facts/history, reference to empowering provision, purpose and conditions of that provision, and application of law to facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For reasons: state authority, history (who applied, any representations), list facts relied upon, give empowering provision reference and purpose, apply law to facts. Repeat this process for subordinate decisions. Keep simple matters short; address core dispute thoroughly.

rubrics_metrics.name: What adequate written reasons should include
rubrics_metrics.description: Adequate reasons should explain the decision-maker’s jurisdiction/authority, the relevant facts and history, the empowering provision and its purpose/conditions, any relevant case law interpretation, and the application of law to the facts leading to the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure reasons so that an affected person can see why the decision was taken and what factual and legal basis supports it. The Guide provides a sample decision letter illustrating these elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: If reasons are not given automatically — informing the right to request reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: If departmental policy is not to provide reasons automatically, the administrator must inform the person of their right to request reasons under the AJA and the regulations (e.g., how to request and the time limit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a clear paragraph after the decision that cites the relevant AJA provision (e.g., section 3(2)(e)), states the time limit (example: within 90 days), gives the address to submit the request, and explains the information to include in the request (reference to decision, which rights were adversely affected, full contact details).

rubrics_metrics.name: Request-for-reasons formalities (contents of a valid request)
rubrics_metrics.description: A request for reasons should refer to the decision, identify which rights are alleged to have been adversely affected, and provide the requester’s full name, postal address and, if available, telephone and fax numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Guide notes that the draft regulations set out more detailed formal requirements and administrators must follow those formalities when processing requests for reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice on legal remedies (what to include in decision letters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions must include information on available remedies: if an internal appeal exists, provide contact details, time limit to lodge the appeal, and any prescribed forms; if no internal appeal, identify the court with jurisdiction and the time limit for review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attach appeal forms where prescribed. In the example the Social Assistance Act appeal period is 90 days. Always state the remedy procedures clearly so the recipient knows how to challenge the decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhaustion of internal remedies before judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: Where internal remedies (appeals or reviews) are available, administrators and applicants should be aware of rules regarding exhaustion of those remedies prior to approaching a court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part 7 discusses exhaustion; administrators should advise applicants of internal channels and time limits to encourage resolution within administrative structures before judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limits for judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: There are statutory time limits for instituting judicial review (the Guide discusses time limits in Part 7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrators should state relevant time limits in decision letters; applicants must be informed of deadlines to bring review proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative action may be reviewed by a court on grounds such as unlawfulness, unreasonableness, and failure to follow fair procedures (and other grounds detailed in Part 7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrators must be mindful of these grounds when making decisions and ensure authority, reasonableness, and procedural fairness to reduce exposure to review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public participation & consultation for decisions affecting the public (section 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: For decisions affecting the public, the AJA requires broader consultation/notice (section 4) — administrators must consult the public before important decisions are taken and follow public-participation procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the AJA’s public-consultation requirements and the Guide’s examples on how to inform and consult communities; ensure the process is open and transparent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Batho Pele service-delivery principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Eight Batho Pele principles guide public service delivery: regularly consult customers; set realistic service standards; increase access to services; ensure courtesy; provide accurate and up-to-date information; increase openness and transparency about service delivery; remedy failures and mistakes; and give value for money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The AJA complements Batho Pele. Administrators should adopt customer-oriented behaviour (e.g., courtesy, apology for mistakes) and involve front-line staff in improving service delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality — avoid bias and prejudice
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions must be made and seen to be made impartially; the AJA requires reasonable and procedurally fair actions to guard against actual or apparent bias or prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrators should ensure no favouritism or unfair prejudice in decisions and document the decision-making process to demonstrate impartiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive decisions must be clearly communicated
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where a decision is favorable (a grant or licence), administrators must inform the applicant clearly and state the decision (including amounts, conditions and duration) to avoid claims of failure to make a clear decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the grant, amount, duration/conditions and any subordinate decisions in one-sentence main/subordinate decision lines as in the template.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting on own authority requires notice and opportunity to make representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the State initiates administrative action (not in response to an application), administrators must give adequate notice of the nature and purpose of the proposed action so affected persons can make representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include withdrawal of an existing grant — give affected person the chance to respond before final action is taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary awards and interim decisions are covered by the AJA
rubrics_metrics.description: Temporary awards (e.g., disability grants for a fixed period) affect rights and therefore fall under the AJA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat temporary awards with the same procedural and reasons obligations as permanent awards where they affect rights or expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make factual enquiries and, where appropriate, take extra steps in line with Batho Pele
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrators should verify information (not rely solely on hearsay) and where appropriate go the 'extra mile' (e.g., visiting an applicant) to obtain responses and promote responsive service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not always legally required, such steps promote fairness and may reduce risk of error or later challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical drafting details and formalities for decision letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Decision letters should include: administrator’s address (letterhead), date, file reference, mailing instruction, recipient details, salutation, subject, statement of purpose, the decision sentence(s), reasons, advice on remedies, complimentary closing, signature, name/job title, department, enclosures and writer’s initials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the provided sample layout and checklist (the Guide annotates an example letter) to ensure completeness and compliance with AJA minima.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs orders: include only where empowered and state particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: If the empowering provision allows or requires a cost order, the decision must state the amount, who must pay, by what date, and attach any required assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only make cost orders where the law authorises; include detail and attach any assessment supporting the cost.
